synopsis: The booklet defines useful visuals as drawings that expose dependencies and gaps, not decoration; it found no credible basis for claiming that any one format universally earns engineering reviewers’ trust [f16469, f9476, f9864, f16470]. It recommends dividing the work among six kinds: layered roadmaps with gates, claim-to-evidence maps, coverage maps, architecture views, probabilistic schedules and risk views [f16473, f16474, f16475, f16476, f16478, f16479, f16480]. Coverage gaps should remain visibly blank rather than disappear into an “85% coverage” score, and simulation credibility should be mapped into supported and unsupported regions with physical evidence rather than reduced to “95% accurate” or a green dashboard [f9880, f8019]. Schedule communication should show distributions or confidence windows, P50, P80 and deadline probability; risk heat maps may serve familiarity but must not drive prioritization because of documented ranking defects [f9889, f9863, f9894, f9895]. Evidence is narrower than a general trust claim: individual experiments found decision or comprehension benefits, decorative-graph persuasion failed to replicate, and uncertainty-display effects depend on context; plain charts and words should expose caveats, while a pilot traffic light should show both the trusted envelope and failures [f9482, f9858, f9484, f9892, f8020, f9920].
